items.title: Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million
items.summary:
Angela Huffman , a sixth-generation farmer, spent 15 years in agriculture policy in Columbus, OH , and Washington, DC. But her focus lately has been 10 miles from her Wharton, OH , sheep farm.

On June 4, Huffman picked up her local newspaper, the Daily Chief-Union. The above-the-fold headline revealed a developer was eyeing a $900 million data center in nearby Upper Sandusky.

The headline "stopped me cold," Huffman says. The proposal would have planted a 146-acre Smartland Energy data center campus, with a natural gas power plant, on the north edge of town.

"We were already worried about a big development coming in and extracting the town's resources," Huffman tells Realtor.com® . Townsfolk were already concerned after another recent proposal for a soybean processing plant.

"What does that do to the community?" she says.

Huffman, CEO of Farm Action, says her family has owned its nearby farm for six generations. Organizing concerned neighbors, they began filling planning commission meetings and peppering officials with questions about the impact of the development. They also questioned if it should be approved on industrial zoning, as neighbors had hoped. A petition opposing the project drew 1,100 signatures.

Many residents worried about how such a major project could change their rural way of life. And Upper Sandusky wasn't alone. 

Ohio was the heart of data center resistance in the midterms. Voters in 18 of its 88 counties backed 21 bans or restrictions on development of those projects. One of those was in Upper Sandusky, where voters approved a charter amendment…
items.t: Ohio Becomes the Epicenter of Data Center Backlash After Tax Credits Cost State’s Schools $374 Million

items.title: Rents Rise Annually for First Time in 3 Years as Multifamily Building Boom Stalls
items.summary:
The median asking rent posted its first annual increase in more than three years in October, fueled by a sharp nationwide pullback in multifamily construction.

October marks the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly rental report . The increase was modest, with the median asking rent rising by just $1 to $1,692, but the underlying data suggests more hikes could follow. 

Larger units drove the rebound. Two-bedrooms led the way, with median asking rent rising 0.3% year over year to $1,889, followed by one-bedrooms, which edged up 0.1% to $1,566. 

Meanwhile, studio rents continued to lag, falling 1.2% from October 2025 to $1,411.

"I see this as the market beginning to rebalance,"  Lissette Calderon , CEO of Neology Group , a Miami-based real estate development firm, tells Realtor.com. "We had an extraordinary amount of new supply delivered over the last few years, and it takes time for that inventory to be absorbed. With construction slowing and demand for rental housing remaining strong, I expect rent growth to gradually return, particularly in markets where employment and household growth continue to support housing demand." 

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu confirms that last month's rent turnaround hinges on a shifting supply pipeline.

The post-pandemic multifamily construction boom of 2021–22 flooded the market with fresh rental units completed in 2023–25, keeping prices in check.

Now, a broad cooling in multifamily construction is easing downward pressure on rent, just as high mortgage rates…
items.t: Rents Rise Annually for First Time in 3 Years as Multifamily Building Boom Stalls

items.title: Study Finds a Nearly 50% Drop in Renters Becoming Homeowners Since 2009
items.summary:
As economic pressures continue to rise, a shocking new study has found that the share of renters who convert to homeownership has fallen 46% since 2009.

TransUnion, a leader in global information and insights, released its 2027 Personal and Commercial Lines Annual Insurance Outlook on Tuesday, which focuses on what the insurance industry needs to stay profitable in a changing market.

The report states that personal line underwriting has been strong throughout this year, but companies need to assess their strategies going forward as fewer people buy cars and homes , therefore reducing the pool of potential policyholders.

According to the report, the share of renters who convert to homeownership was 3.9% in 2025, a sharp decline from 7.2% in 2009.

This represents a shocking 46% decrease in the share of renters transitioning to homeownership in just 14 years.

Combined with a 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors®, which stated that the median age of first-time buyers climbed from 33 to 40 in just five years, TransUnion concluded that the pool of potential policyholders is shrinking.

The decrease in renters buying homes goes back to affordability and economic pressure, according to Ryan Thomson of The Assumable Guy .

“Renters didn't stop wanting to own. Rates tripled and prices kept climbing, so the monthly number stopped working,” Thomson tells Realtor.com® . “In Colorado Springs, where I sell, 71% of households could afford a median-priced home in 2019. By 2023, it was 25.3%. So renters stay put. Or they move wherever the payment still works.”…
items.t: Study Finds a Nearly 50% Drop in Renters Becoming Homeowners Since 2009

items.title: Daniel Craig Stepped Away From James Bond Role To Spend More Time at Home
items.summary:
Daniel Craig first stepped into the role of James Bond 20 years ago, and now, he has officially passed the duties along to someone new: Robert Pattinson .

Craig made his 007 debut in the 2006 film “Casino Royale” and held the legendary gig for 15 years. He had originally planned to play the British spy for four films, but ended up having a successful five-movie run with “Quantum Solace” (2008), “Skyfall” (2012), “Spectre” (2015), and “No Time To Die” (2021).

In addition to filming one more motion picture than he had planned, Craig, 58, has spoken out about how physically demanding it is to be James Bond. In the time between the last two films, he told The Sunday Times he was “getting old.”

“I’m creaky,” he admitted in the 2019 interview. In 2024, he told The New York Times , “I find it really hard, this job, and it gets harder as I get older.”

Beyond the grueling stunts and action required for each installment, the role demanded a huge time commitment that pulled Craig away from his family.

Daniel Craig's reign as James Bond ended with the 2021 film "No Time to Die." It was recently announced Robert Pattinson will take on the iconic role. (Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Omega)

items.title: Wisconsin Couple Seek To Enforce $1,350 Judgment Against Each of Their Neighbors in HOA Dispute
items.summary:
A neighborhood outside Green Bay , WI, is locked in a yearslong legal battle, as one couple is now taking legal action against their neighbors to collect a $200,000 settlement.

What began as a dispute over a backyard fence has turned into an ongoing series of lawsuits, with neighbors being forced to pay $1,350 each in a settlement —and those who haven’t are now being taken to court.

The case is centered around Michael and Lisa Newman and their five children, who reside in the Nazcr Trac neighborhood in De Pere , WI. After some of their children were diagnosed with autism, the Newmans wanted to build a fence around their backyard, as they wanted the children to be able to play outside safely.

Citing the children’s diagnoses and that two of their children “demonstrated significant risk of elopement,” according to a press release from the Metropolitan Milwaukee Fair Housing Council, the Newmans wrote to the Nazcr Trac Property Owners Association (NTPOA) to request an accommodation to the subdivision’s “no fence” rule.

Neither the initial request, sent in July 2019, nor a subsequent request in December 2020, which included information about the association’s legal obligation to consider an accommodation due to the children’s disabilities, were answered by the association.

In August 2021, the Newmans filed a lawsuit against the association in federal court, alleging that it had discriminated based on disability, a violation of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. A judge granted a preliminary injunction in May 2022 that prohibits the NTPOA from enforcing the rule, and the…
items.t: Wisconsin Couple Seek To Enforce $1,350 Judgment Against Each of Their Neighbors in HOA Dispute

items.title: Buyers Need Cheaper Homes. Airbnb Is Putting $1 Million Toward Finding New Solutions.
items.summary:
For many Americans these days, affordable housing is still out of reach. 

Airbnb is stepping up to the plate to try to change that.

The company announced a $1 million annual Housing Innovation Prize to support innovators and entrepreneurs who are striving to make it faster, easier, and cheaper to buy homes. It plans to distribute one award per year over a five-year period.

The $1 million prizes are intended for U.S.-based companies and nonprofits with ideas that are already in the works but need funding to succeed. These may include factory-built homes , faster construction sides, expedited permitting , or easier financing for new homes.

“Airbnb started as a way to help my co-founders pay their rent. Today millions of people do the same. Now we are helping to finance the building of housing in communities nationwide. We want to encourage others, through this prize, to think more creatively and ambitiously about home building and delivering affordability. Necessity is the mother of invention,” said Nathan Blecharczyk , Airbnb’s co-founder and chief strategy officer, in a recent press release . 

While Airbnb’s efforts are a step in the right direction, experts agree that addressing the affordability crisis as a whole requires more funding, innovation, and collaboration across the industry. 

The need for innovation 

Airbnb's initiative brings renewed attention to the need for more housing in the U.S., and finding ways to build it more efficiently and affordably is becoming increasingly important.

Realtor.com® data shows how serious the housing supply gap has become.…

items.title: Abandoned Property for Sale: How To Buy an Abandoned Home
items.summary:
Buying an abandoned property can be a bargain for homebuyers —if you can actually find such a property.

Properties that are unclaimed by their owners are potential low-cost purchases that might be attractive to prospective homebuyers. They certainly have become all the rage on TikTok , with influencers snatching up properties left and right and sharing their renovation journeys.

Still, "abandoned house for sale" isn't a sign you're likely to see on the roadside. (There might actually be laws against that!)

An abandoned property is usually a property whose original owner is no longer in possession of the home. Due to the owner's financial difficulties, the house is typically run-down and in desperate need of repair. If the law in your area allows you to claim this type of home and you're handy, it might be worth investigating.

However, some abandoned homes for sale can turn out to be in good condition, with the owner hoping to unload the property before foreclosure . This could provide the right buyer with an opportunity to purchase the abandoned property or unclaimed home at a discount—and possibly a significant return on investment if you later flip it.

How to buy an abandoned property for sale near you 

Purchasing an abandoned or unclaimed property involves following the same procedures as buying any other piece of real estate. Before setting out on your journey to find an abandoned home, review your financial situation.

Remember, there will be additional expenses over and above the original sale price of the property. A pre-qualification from your bank or lender…
items.t: Abandoned Property for Sale: How To Buy an Abandoned Home

items.title: U.S. Chamber Backs Capital Gains Tax Exclusion Bill Aimed To Reduce Taxes on Profits From Home Sales
items.summary:
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has announced support for reducing taxes on the profits homeowners make on the sale of their home, saying it could stimulate more home sales.

Raising the capital gains tax exclusion—something hundreds of members of Congress and a number of real estate groups have pushed for this year—is one key lever that Washington, DC hasn't yet pulled. It could have major implications for the housing market, the Chamber said.

"Capital gains taxes tend to distort housing choices by discouraging individuals from selling their homes because of changing family or health circumstances," the group said . "And the taxation of capital gains in excess of exemption caps creates inequities between homeowners with different job circumstances and those living in different parts of the country."

The most visible effort in Congress comes from the More Homes on the Market Act , sponsored by Rep. Jimmy Panetta (R-CA), which would double the current exclusion. Realtor.com® has reached out to his office for comment.

Both the Senate and the House have versions of the bill, which are almost identical . The Chamber said that bill offers a "reasonable, cost-effective solution" to spur more home sales.

The two versions have picked up 186 sponsors and cosponsors in Congress, including large numbers of Democrats and Republicans. Earlier this year, Panetta acknowledged the push faces resistance. A congressional analysis from last year estimated such a change could deprive the government of $46.4 billion in tax revenue. Even a more targeted approach, like raising the exclusion…
items.t: U.S. Chamber Backs Capital Gains Tax Exclusion Bill Aimed To Reduce Taxes on Profits From Home Sales

items.title: Homebuilder Confidence Hits New 14-Year Low as High Mortgage Rates and Inflation Take a Toll
items.summary:
U.S. homebuilders are feeling increasingly pessimistic about the new-construction sector of the housing market amid mounting affordability concerns. 

Builder confidence in new single-family home sales fell three points month over month, bringing the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) down to 25, a new 14-year low . Any reading below 50 reflects the industry's negative view of the market.

This is the lowest HMI reading since April 2012. For context, builder sentiment has now remained below 40 for 19 consecutive months.

"Strange times indeed—home prices are at record highs, the stock market has soared in recent years, employment is holding strong, and yet builders feel pessimistic about building homes," Jeff Ostrowski, a housing market analyst at Bankrate, tells Realtor.com® .

NAHB Chairman Bill Owens attributes the sharp downturn to high mortgage rates, ongoing inflation pressure, elevated energy and material costs, rising labor shortages, and sidelined buyers.

"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy," says Owens. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."

Last week, Freddie Mac reported that the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11%, tracking lower bond yields, yet the latest hotter-than-expected inflation print could make the relief…
items.t: Homebuilder Confidence Hits New 14-Year Low as High Mortgage Rates and Inflation Take a Toll

The 29-year-old real estate agent, who shot to fame alongside her parents, Todd and Julie Chrisley , on their reality TV show, "Chrisley Knows Best," announced on Oct. 27 that she was both pregnant and engaged to Galanis, who is 27 years her senior and served time behind bars alongside her father.

Days later, it was revealed that they are actually married, with People reporting that they said "I do" on July 14—just one year after beginning their romance.

Then, it was reported that the couple had snapped up a $2.2 million family home in Nashville. 

Now, the TV personality has revealed that she is expected to welcome her son in just "10 weeks" in an Instagram post, in which she joked she was "a little more than half baked" while she and her spouse chewed on chocolate chips. 

Savannah Chrisley has confirmed that her due date is in "10 weeks"—after announcing that she and her husband, Jason Galanis, had tied the knot and were expecting a baby boy. (Instagram) 

"Okay so maybe a little more than half baked. Can’t believe we only have 10 weeks until baby boy arrives! Your daddy and I cannot wait to meet you, sweet boy," she captioned the post.

In the carousel of snaps, the couple could be seen embracing as they held up their sonogram photos. 

In the caption, she revealed that her mom had baked the cookies for the special photoshoot. 

Just two weeks ago, Chrisley announced the gender of her child…
items.t: Savannah Chrisley Reveals Her Due Date—Weeks After Announcing She and Husband Jason Galanis are Having a Boy

items.title: Late Film Critic Rex Reed Bought His Dakota Apartment for $30,000 in 1969—Now It’s Listed for Nearly $6 Million
items.summary:

The two-bedroom, two-bathroom abode spans about 2,000 square feet—and decades of cultural history.

The dwelling has certainly been used for exactly that. According to the New York Times , Reed hosted guests including Hollywood legends Lauren Bacall , Boris Karloff , and Truman Capote .

items.title: Home Depot Taps Longtime Exec for CEO as Company Faces ‘Frozen Housing Market’
items.summary:
Home Depot COO Richard McPhail was announced as the company's new CEO on Tuesday, ahead of the home improvement giant's third-quarter earnings call. McPhail will take over on Nov. 23.

McPhail is taking the reins from Ted Decker , who will stay on as chairman. Decker stepped into the role in 2022. 

McPhail has been with Home Depot since 2005 and previously served as executive vice president and chief financial officer.

Meanwhile, Ann-Marie Campbell was named president and chief operating officer. Campbell began her career with the retailer 41 years ago, as a sales associate and most recently served as an executive vice president in charge of U.S. stores as well as Home Depot Canada, Home Depot Mexico, and Pro sales and services.

On Tuesday, during its third-quarter earnings call , the company reported better than expected quarterly revenue of $43.4 billion, up 4.9% from a year ago.

In remarks during the call, McPhail said Home Depot is “continuing to gain market share in a pressured housing market."

During the company's second-quarter earnings call in August, McPhail spoke of the "consumer uncertainty" around the housing market.

"While consumer uncertainty and housing affordability continue to pressure demand for larger home improvement projects, we remain focused on what we can control, our strategy of driving our core and culture, delivering a frictionless, interconnected experience, and winning the pro," he said. 

New CEO Richard McPhail said during the company's Q3 earnings call that Home Depot is "continuing to gain market share in a pressured housing market."…
items.t: Home Depot Taps Longtime Exec for CEO as Company Faces ‘Frozen Housing Market’

items.title: Builders Are Slashing Mortgage Rates To Win Buyers, but Hold Firm on Sticker Prices
items.summary:
Prices for new homes have been stagnant for years. That leaves room for potential homebuyers if they're on the hunt for good incentives.

The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on new homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers, relying on rate buydowns and other incentives as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate stays above 7% .

The median listing price for new builds hit $451,071 in the third quarter. It's been right around that number since late 2023. Builders are starting fewer homes in the inflation-plagued economy. 

Increased labor and material costs and decreased buyer demand led to the completion rate of new single-family homes falling 11.0% year over year in September.

Meanwhile, existing-home prices came in 1.5% below 2025 levels, landing at $402,883. New homes have to compete with existing homes for buyers, and the rise in existing-home sales shows that some cost-conscious buyers who might have built new are choosing existing, instead. Existing-home sales just hit a 16-year low .

"Builders were quicker to adjust to the realities of muted buyer demand in this high-rate environment, while existing-home sellers had pricing expectations based on the market from 2021 and 2022 that were slower to dissolve," Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner writes in the report. "The overall price softness we’ve seen through 2026 is driven primarily by the existing-home segment."

That's led to more builders and sellers tempering their expectations. Resellers cut prices on 21.6% of homes this…
items.t: Builders Are Slashing Mortgage Rates To Win Buyers, but Hold Firm on Sticker Prices

items.title: Can America Build More Housing Without Gutting Historic Protections? Inside the Senate’s Permitting Battle
items.summary:
A sweeping permitting reform package moved closer to a final Senate vote Monday, when lawmakers voted 70–27 to limit debate on legislation that could weaken a federal safeguard for historic places.

At issue is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act , which requires federal agencies to consider how projects they fund, approve, or permit might affect historic properties—and consult with those affected before proceeding.

The proposed changes would exempt most projects whose only federal connection is financial assistance, while imposing tighter deadlines and restricting legal challenges.

As the nation confronts a shortage of 4.03 million homes and an aging energy grid, supporters argue that reducing regulatory hurdles will accelerate infrastructure development. But preservation advocates warn the changes could leave communities with less influence over what gets built—and what gets lost.

"Preservation is not a hindrance to progress," Heather Veneziano , director of Tulane University's Historic Preservation Program , told Realtor.com® during a recent walking interview through Bayou St. John , one of New Orleans' oldest neighborhoods .

Rather than keeping neighborhoods frozen in time, she argued, preservation can help communities determine how they evolve.

"Keeping things static is impossible," Veneziano said.

Preserving the past without preventing the future 

New Orleans provides a particularly salient standpoint from which to understand Veneziano’s perspective.

The city is home to 26 nationally recognized historic districts encompassing more than…
items.t: Can America Build More Housing Without Gutting Historic Protections? Inside the Senate’s Permitting Battle

items.title: The Homeownership Gap Between Young and Old Americans Has Doubled—These Cities Reveal Why
items.summary:
The homeownership gap between younger and older Americans has more than doubled over the past four decades, with some of the nation's most expensive cities seeing the sharpest increases , according to a new report.

The analysis, from the Urban Institute , finds that nationally just 43% of households headed by adults aged 25 to 35 owned their homes in 2024, compared with 79% of those headed by adults 65 and older. The 35.8-percentage-point difference is more than twice the 17.5-point gap recorded in 1980.

But that divide pales in comparison to the gaping chasm in some of America's most expensive metropolitan areas. Between 1980 and 2024, the homeownership gap grew by 29 percentage points in Denver , 23 points in New York City , and 22 points in San Francisco , compared with 18.3 points nationally.

But those widening gaps also expose a deeper economic trade-off: The cities offering young Americans the greatest opportunities to earn more may be the very places preventing them from building wealth through homeownership

"The cities with the strongest labor markets tend to be the least affordable, so some will take the better job and rent indefinitely, giving up equity accumulation," explains Hannah Jones , senior economist at Realtor.com® . "Others will pass up higher-paying roles or move to cheaper, lower-opportunity markets in order to buy."

How Denver and New York arrived at the same divide 

In 1980, younger households in Denver were nearly as likely as their older counterparts to own a home.

At the time, 55% of households headed by adults aged 25 to 35 owned their…
items.t: The Homeownership Gap Between Young and Old Americans Has Doubled—These Cities Reveal Why

items.title: La Gorce Island Point Lot Overlooking Biscayne Bay Is Listed for an Eye-Watering $170 Million
items.summary:
A spectacular waterfront mansion on Miami ’s guard-gated La Gorce Island has hit the market for a jaw-dropping $170 million.

Built in 2015, the legacy estate is reportedly owned by Betsy Sherman , wife of George Sherman , the late former chairman of Campbell’s. If the property fetches anywhere near its asking price, it would rank among Miami’s most expensive home sales ever, according to The Wall Street Journal .

The Shermans purchased the property for just $17 million in 2006 and custom-built the sprawling 18,213-square-foot estate , which now claims the top spot on the Realtor.com® weekly list of the most expensive homes .

Boasting 320 feet of Biscayne Bay frontage, the residence was designed to capture spectacular sunset views from nearly every room.

Interior highlights include an expansive great room with sliding glass doors that open to the outdoor living area, a formal dining room, a modern kitchen, and a bar.

A sculptural, curved glass staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, where a lavish primary retreat features a private terrace overlooking the bay.

Additional amenities include a fitness center, bunk room, pool, four-car garage, and deep-water dock designed to accommodate yachts.

More spectacular mansions to make the week's most expensive homes list include a Utah mountain retreat under construction, an oceanfront estate in Hawaii with sweeping Pacific Ocean views, and a rebuilt Palm Beach, FL, sanctuary.

items.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
items.summary:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.

items.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says
items.summary:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% this month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.
